stories.headline: US-IRAN STRIKES SEND OIL ABOVE $85, RATTLE STOCKS TO OPEN THE WEEK
stories.body: The U.S. and Iran exchanged strikes for the first time in roughly a month, sending WTI crude up 2.6% to $85.60 and Brent above $90 on fears of disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The S&P 500 fell 0.33% to 7,686 and the Dow dropped 374 points (-0.7%), though both indexes still closed out August with gains.
stories.explain: The Strait of Hormuz carries roughly a fifth of global oil supply, so any threat to it prices in a risk premium immediately, well before actual barrels are disrupted. That premium feeds straight into headline inflation expectations, which raises the odds the Fed leans hawkish at its next meeting — the same mechanism that pushed Treasury yields higher today and pressured equity valuations.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD TOPS 4.75%, HIGHEST SINCE JANUARY 2025
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield pushed above 4.75% intraday, its highest level since January 2025, as rising oil prices reinforced bets the Fed will hike rates in September. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, speaking at the G20 conference, said 'secular stagnation seems like a description of a past long ago,' reinforcing the hawkish tone he struck at Jackson Hole on Friday.
stories.explain: Long-end yields price the market's expected path for the fed funds rate plus a term premium, not the current policy rate itself, so hawkish commentary and an oil-driven inflation scare both get repriced into the 10-year immediately. Higher yields raise the discount rate used to value future corporate cash flows, which is the direct channel through which today's bond move pressured stock valuations.

stories.headline: GOLD SINKS TO $4,483 DESPITE MIDEAST ESCALATION AS RATE-HIKE ODDS DOMINATE
stories.body: Gold fell about 1% to $4,483 an ounce even as fighting between the U.S. and Iran intensified — a break from gold's usual safe-haven script, as rising real yields from Fed rate-hike bets outweighed the geopolitical risk premium.
stories.explain: Gold pays no coupon or dividend, so its cost of carry is set by the real (inflation-adjusted) interest rate: when nominal yields rise faster than inflation expectations, real yields climb and holding zero-yield gold gets relatively more expensive. Today that real-rate effect from Warsh's hawkish tone dominated the safe-haven bid that would normally come from a Middle East flare-up, which is why gold and oil moved in opposite directions on the same headline.

stories.headline: S&P 500 CLOSES AUGUST UP 2.6% DESPITE MONDAY'S GEOPOLITICAL PULLBACK
stories.body: Monday's 0.33% decline snapped a strong run, but the S&P 500 still finished August with a 2.6% gain, powered by strong big-tech earnings through most of the month. The Nasdaq 100 slipped roughly 0.4% to around 29,433 as investors rotated out of risk on the Iran headlines.
stories.explain: A single risk-off session inside a positive month is a reminder to separate the news-driven daily move from the underlying trend: August's gain was built on an earnings-driven rerating of mega-cap tech, and today's pullback is a reaction to a fresh geopolitical shock rather than a reversal of that trend — the distinction matters for whether investors should expect the dip to persist into September.

stories.headline: NCAA TOURNAMENT TO EXPAND TO 76 TEAMS STARTING 2026-27
stories.body: The NCAA confirmed the men's basketball tournament will expand from 68 to 76 teams beginning with the 2026-27 season, with the same expansion applied to the women's tournament. In coaching news, Florida's Todd Golden signed a six-year, $49.5 million extension after last season's title run.

stories.headline: 76ERS LAND LEBRON AND JAYLEN BROWN; GIANNIS HEADS TO MIAMI
stories.body: Philadelphia turned itself into a title contender this summer, keeping LeBron James and trading for Jaylen Brown, while Giannis Antetokounmpo signed with the Miami Heat to team up with Bam Adebayo. Golden State also re-signed Draymond Green to a one-year, $27.7 million deal as the league's superstar landscape reshapes ahead of training camp.

stories.headline: AARON DONALD UN-RETIRES, SIGNS BACK WITH RAMS AS LEAGUE FINALIZES 53-MAN ROSTERS
stories.body: Aaron Donald is coming out of retirement to rejoin the Los Angeles Rams on a one-year, $20 million deal after all 32 teams cut down to 53-man rosters over the weekend, releasing 1,184 players leaguewide. Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes is dealing with a knee issue that has coach Andy Reid unsure of his Week 1 status.

stories.headline: WEEK 1 HEADLINED BY BOISE STATE-OREGON AS SEASON SHIFTS INTO GEAR
stories.body: With Week 0 in the books, the marquee Week 1 matchup is No. 25 Boise State visiting Oregon on Saturday, with several analysts picking the Broncos to make the College Football Playoff field over the Ducks. Most of the country's Week 1 slate is set for Labor Day weekend, Sept. 4-7.

sports.detail: No. 17 Huskies wrapped preseason camp; season opener is the Apple Cup vs. Washington State at Husky Stadium, Sunday, Sept. 6 at 1 p.m. PT on NBC — third-year coach Jedd Fisch's team opens Big Ten play later in September.

Coming off a 16-17 (7-13 Big Ten) season under Danny Sprinkle, the Huskies lost forward Hannes Steinbach to the Charlotte Hornets in the NBA Draft and are rebuilding the roster for 2026-27; regular season tips off in November.

Seattle finalized its 53-man roster over the weekend and locked up two building blocks, signing DT Leonard Williams to a three-year, $90 million extension and CB Devon Witherspoon to a four-year extension on Monday.

Coming off a 60-win, third-best-record season in the East, Detroit remains in a contract standoff with All-NBA center Jalen Duren and is banking on internal development over a big trade ahead of training camp.
Shut out 7-0 by the Blue Jays on Sunday, dropping Seattle to 64-73, third in the AL West. Next up: at the Red Sox tonight, 6:45 p.m. ET at Fenway (George Kirby vs. Parlo Tolle).

deepDive.title: Why Gold Fell While Oil Spiked: Real Yields and the Cost of Carry
content: Today's brief has an apparent contradiction sitting right in the market data: the U.S. and Iran traded strikes for the first time in a month, WTI crude jumped 2.6% to $85.60, and the 10-year Treasury yield pushed above 4.75% for the first time since January 2025 — yet gold, the asset investors are taught to buy when geopolitical risk spikes, fell about 1% to $4,483. That is not noise. It is the market telling you which variable is actually driving prices today, and it is not the headline risk everyone is reading about.

Gold pays no coupon, no dividend, and no rent — its entire cost of holding it is the return you give up by not holding something that does pay, typically a Treasury bond. That opportunity cost is best measured by the real interest rate: the nominal yield minus expected inflation. When Fed Chair Warsh's hawkish tone pushes nominal yields up faster than inflation expectations move, real yields rise, and gold gets mechanically more expensive to hold relative to bonds. That real-rate effect from today's rate-hike repricing outweighed the safe-haven bid the Iran conflict would normally generate.

This is not a new pattern — it played out through most of 2022, when gold traded flat to down for months despite the Ukraine invasion, because the Fed's aggressive hiking cycle was pushing real yields sharply higher at the same time. What most people miss is that gold's 'safe haven' behavior is conditional: it works when a crisis lowers expected rates (a flight to safety that also pulls down growth and rate expectations) but fails when a crisis raises them, as an oil-driven inflation scare does. Direction of the real-rate move, not the presence of geopolitical risk, is the deciding variable.

For a portfolio, the actionable takeaway is to stop asking 'is there geopolitical risk today' and start asking 'which way are real yields moving because of it.' Watching TIPS-implied breakevens alongside the nominal 10-year gives a cleaner read than either yield alone. Going into a week where the Fed's rate path is already in play and oil has a fresh supply-risk premium attached, gold's next move will hinge on whether the inflation scare or the rate-hike scare wins out — if breakevens rise faster than nominal yields, real yields fall and gold's recent slide likely reverses.
